column2: On Ebbe's third or fourth day, he attends what will be the college's last theatrical production, Medea, written and directed by Robert Duncan, with every member of the community onstage; Ebbe was probably one of the only spectators. The whole community acting; Ebbe probably the only audience

Horowitz walks to Street Hall wondering whether he will be taught to draw like the Old Masters or to assemble squares and circles into cats and dogs; he sits down in the silent room; Albers announces that his eyes will be educated and that this will be a course in seeing and thinking. Words: Albers informs the students that their eyes will be educated and that his course will be a course in seeing and thinking. Atmosphere: A hushed room, the novice's surprise and fascination. Stakes: The student's expectations overturned: drawing becomes a spiritual quest.
On Ebbe's third or fourth day, the whole community performs Medea, written and directed by Duncan; Ebbe is among the only spectators. Stakes: The college's theatrical swan song

The very day of the announcement or the next, Ebbe joins the group leaving for San Francisco, throws his bags in the trunk, and jumps into the back of one of the cars; as they leave, he turns around and sees Olson on all fours, frantically pulling the weeds from the road that led to the college. Olson on all fours weeding the road

Huss plans to join Duncan and his partner Jess in San Francisco to continue the Medea trilogy, find former students (Alexander, Field, Rumaker), and collaborate with Ginsberg and Kerouac, whose work appeared in the seventh and last issue of the Black Mountain College Review. Last issue: No. 7 of the BMC Review

Night, candles, tea from reused tea bags. Olson stands up: “The college is closing.” Faces in shock. He explains: they need paying students, they cannot pay themselves, and no money will come. One student, then another, offers to write to his grandmother; Olson waves it away. Beer, a quiet party; Dita Frauenglass takes two photographs. Olson gives vague details: the farm and the upper campus will be sold, and he will stay to clean up. Huss announces San Francisco; others New York or Chicago; one by one everyone goes back to his cottage. Words: “The college is closing”; “We need paying students”; “We've got no money, no money's coming in, nobody'll send us money”; offers to write to grandmother Atmosphere: Candlelight, shock, then relaxation over beer Stakes: The end of the college, a twenty-four-year adventure

The car in the convoy for San Francisco pulls away; Ebbe, in the back, turns around and sees Olson on all fours, frantically pulling the weeds from the road that led to the college. Atmosphere: An image of a fall, solitary, absurd, and heartbreaking Stakes: The last image of the college, through its last student

A spoof in which Reinhardt appears as “Adolph M. Pure, famous Anti-Post-Abstract-Impressionist,” painting with a black fluid injected into foam rubber and declaring that the purer your art, the less you can give. Despite constant disagreements, they liked each other and argued in the greatest good humor. Black injected into foam rubber (a parodic fiction)

A superb portrait of Elaine with arms spread, sitting in the corner of a flowered sofa at Porter's, in a flowing, flamboyant red dress; her direct, slightly skeptical gaze illuminates one facet of her personality. Flowered sofa, red dress

The following spring, Fitz holds court at the Cedar Tavern to organize the fall exhibition “7 Contemporary Painters.” To save on shipping, the canvases are taken off their stretchers, rolled up, and loaded into Fitz's station wagon to Amarillo. Elaine flies there, her first sight of the Southwest, probably with an excursion to New Mexico. Despite low prices ($2,000 for the largest canvas), the only buyer is Fitz himself. $2,000 for the largest canvas; a single buyer Consequences: Fitz nonetheless mounts another avant-garde exhibition in 1959.

The birth of Joan Ward's child in 1956 is the last straw. Elaine moves to 80 St. Mark's Place; her brothers carry her belongings in wheelbarrows from her studio on 28th Street (more than twenty blocks). The lease stipulated that she was not to live there; a nightclub downstairs played “God awful” music every night from 9 p.m. to 4 a.m.; one brother: “This is a wonderful studio for an artist to go mad in” Consequences: Eighteen years of living apart, without divorce

The couple separates in 1957, a year after Elaine's fiercest portraits (a drawing with the facial features erased, Bill at St. Marks). Consequences: Follows the year of the portraits in which Bill's face is erased or barred with blue

After Sputnik and the failure of the first American launcher, a quick inquiry concludes that scientists come from everywhere and were trained by devoted, unsung teachers whom their students loved, a conclusion that delights Fuller. Consequences: An implicit plea for teaching in the Black Mountain manner

The weaving commissioned from Anni for Temple Emanu-El in Dallas is installed. The same year, a selection of Josef's works is shown at the 4th São Paulo Bienal, at the Museum of Modern Art (September-December).
Anni's textile commission installed at Temple Emanu-El in Dallas; a selection of Josef's work at the IV Bienal de São Paulo (Museu de Arte Moderna, September-December).
Anni's textile commission for Temple Emanu-El is installed
An article in Perspecta, the Yale architecture journal (no. 4, pp. 36-41); an abridged version, “Fabric, the Pliable Plane,” in Craft Horizons, July-August 1958.

Victor D'Amico, director of MoMA's People's Art Center, had attended the 1944 summer session at BMC and remembered her when her name was suggested to him: a first teaching post in 1957, a career still going at the time of the account. Consequences: A vocation as a teacher; she too coaxes her students into learning to see

The magazine founded by Olson and Creeley to loosen the grip of the New Criticism publishes in its final issue Ginsberg's “America,” Kerouac's “From October in the Railroad Earth,” poems by Snyder and McClure, a section of Burroughs's then unpublished Naked Lunch, and a fragment of Selby's unpublished Last Exit to Brooklyn. An issue dated 1957; more interesting to read than Partisan Review or New Directions Consequences: Makes felt Olson's leavening influence on American literature

Issue 7 (fall 1957), 240 pages: Ginsberg as contributing editor, Ginsberg's “America,” Kerouac's “From October in the Railroad Earth,” poems by Snyder, Whalen, and McClure, excerpts from Burroughs's unpublished Naked Lunch (signed “William Lee”) and from Selby's Last Exit to Brooklyn, plus a negative review of Howl by Rumaker, which also savages Kerouac. Blackburn will judge Rumaker's review the most balanced criticism ever written of that poem. Consequences: Creeley sees in it a shift of center and as good a place as any to end. Material for an eighth issue existed, but the college had ceased to exist.

The Cedar Bar crowd, like the Beats in San Francisco, had had enough of hearing Black Mountain and the superiority of its way of life extolled. Oppenheimer claims that in the late '50s he could have signed up twenty young people with money for Black Mountain on any Saturday night at the Cedar, so great were the legend and the appeal of the style.

Williams loads his father's station wagon with books from Jargon, Golden Goose, City Lights, Grove Press, and New Directions and travels the country, a tour never finished according to Duberman, selling the books and reading the work of the “Black Mountain Poets,” spreading their reputation and influence. His father's station wagon; publishers' lists: Jargon, Golden Goose, City Lights, Grove Press, New Directions. Consequences: The spread of the legend and influence of the Black Mountain poets.
A few months after the accident, for many reasons, the college closes for good; Olson carries out the liquidation, holds on to the end, and is the last to leave, in 1957.

A few months after the summer of 1955, the college closes for good; Olson, as rector, settles the affairs of the closing, holds on to the end, and is the last to leave, in 1957. Consequences: The end of the institution after twenty-four years.

One summer day, the married artist goes out to buy cigarettes and supplies at the hardware store; Elaine comes out of her building at the same moment; they walk together; she listens to him with total attention; he invites her for a coffee, she prefers a drink; they talk about their poverty; she quotes her mother, Marie; then they go to his studio, where she examines all his work with total absorption; they become lovers. Elaine wears four-inch platform shoes, tight pants, and a brightly colored blouse; she quotes Marie: “Just take care of the luxuries, the necessities will take care themselves”; in the studio, arms folded, she holds one arm with the other hand, squeezing her breast Consequences: An affair lasting several years; the lover gives up the idea of a bread-and-butter job and pursues his career as an artist
A work included in “Young American Painters” at MoMA and in the Pittsburgh International, two prestigious exhibitions.

After Sputnik, Conant's quasi-official reports on the high schools are so lacking in pedagogical imagination that Goodman regards them as a minor national catastrophe: the motivation of the brightest students is never questioned, and only 15% are said to be “academically talented.” 15% “academically talented”; tests at around twelve to fifteen

An anxious address on the “Problem of Leisure”: with the shorter week and automation, millions of adults might loaf and get into mischief; Douglass calls for a “new ethic” and a new aesthetic. Goodman cites this speech as an example of the verbiage of official spokesmen, masking disappointment and resignation. A quotation calling for a “new ethic” and a “more meaningful existence” Consequences: Goodman makes it the target of his critique: grace is not found by importing a revelation from outside

The summer before his review is published, Goodman hears Ginsberg read a passage from Howl: a litany of imprecations begun pianissimo and ended in a thunderous fortissimo. The audience is excited (“the greatest”); Goodman then asks the poet where, in the ideas, the images, or the rhythm, the justification for this crescendo lay. Ginsberg, crestfallen and furious, admits he had never thought about it. A reading beginning in a low voice and rising gradually to a roar; a young, enthusiastic audience Consequences: Goodman draws from it his distinction between shared excitement and real poetic experience; the formula “You can't howl a gripe”

A 21-year-old reader comes to Goodman's, carrying On the Road. An expressionless, masklike face, a square jaw of suspicious vigilance, a fixed stare of unfelt hostility, teeth grinding against a vague threat; when given attention, his lips split into a small childlike smile. He explains that one must avoid any commitment to an activity, for fear of making the wrong choice. Age 21; a facial mask; molars grinding; a childlike smile when attended to Consequences: Goodman concludes: with no interest in anything, one reaps only “kicks,” the agitation of a stiff body in different cities

Albers argues for simple materials: teaching form and order without a long technical apprenticeship. Quotation: “the Yale students have only two semesters… we have to teach them something about form and order”. Consequences: The birth of a unique approach to teaching sculpture.

Nalle leaves Yale at the end of the 1955-56 academic year; in 1957 Albers introduces a third basic design course, Structural Organization, for third-year architecture students in Yale College, which fills the gap left by Nalle. A course reserved for undergraduate architects in their junior year Consequences: Albers's drawing and color courses become required of all first-year students in architecture and in the design department

Albers hires two trusted former students, Neil Welliver (painter) and Robert Engman (sculptor), full-time to reinvent the design and sculpture courses; Welliver creates an entirely new Basic Design course, Engman rebuilds the sculpture program. Erwin Hauer, a postgraduate sculptor, becomes Engman's assistant, then develops his own course and heads sculpture after Engman's departure in 1962. Albers sees these courses as a chance to propagate the ideas born at the Bauhaus and refined at Black Mountain. Consequences: The design-sculpture program becomes truly revolutionary

Albers, at the end of his career at Yale, hires two former graduate students he trusts to overhaul and relaunch the courses in design (Welliver, a painter) and sculpture (Engman, a sculptor). He first works closely with them to pass on his methods, then gives them a free hand once he is sure they have understood. Full-time posts; Welliver creates an entirely new Basic Design course; Engman builds the sculpture program from scratch. Consequences: The birth of a program the author calls revolutionary, a propagator of Bauhaus and Black Mountain methods.

Albers hires the postgraduate sculptor Erwin Hauer as Engman's assistant; Hauer then develops his own course and takes over the sculpture program after Engman leaves in 1962. Consequences: Hauer teaches a basic course from 1959 on with an approach (modeling bones in clay) that contradicts Albers's dogma, without Albers, no longer heading the school, being able to oppose it.

After the closing, Olson stays on to finalize the financial and psychic affairs: the dispersal of John Rice's library and arrangements for the long-term care of the graves of Jalowetz and of the mathematics professor Max Dehn. Rice's library dispersed; the graves of Jalowetz and Dehn, the beloved and the adored
After 1957 she stops exhibiting and devotes all her attention to education and to helping others open their eyes.
In 1957, Olson tries in vain to sell the pot shop and the adjoining land to a local potter.

The seventh and last issue, which merges Black Mountain poetics with the emerging San Francisco Beat scene, appears when the campus's surrender to financial and intellectual entropy is complete. Consequences: The college closes the same year.

An analysis of an issue of Elle on some seventy women writers, captioned with their numbers of children and novels; Barthes decodes in it the myth of “double parturition.” Captions of the type “Jacqueline Lenoir (deux filles, un roman)”.

Cunningham photographs Asawa working at home with several of her children; in other frames on the contact sheet, baby Adam walks toward the open window or settles into the open wire sculpture on his mother's lap while she keeps working. The complete contact sheet kept at the Imogen Cunningham Trust Consequences: Cunningham chooses the frame of absorption, an image that became iconic

Cunningham photographs Asawa working on her sculptures surrounded by her children; other negatives from the same session show the interruptions removed from the chosen image. Children leafing through picture books, waving a wooden stick, drinking from a bottle; a contact sheet of negatives kept at the Imogen Cunningham Trust Consequences: The chosen image stages a “maternal bohemia” reconciling modernism and motherhood

The toddler Adam, sitting on the floor facing Untitled (AB.029, Continuous Form within a Form, 1956), casts the shadow of his raised arm, stretched toward his mother's hand; the two shadows bisect the painting's radiating curve. A painting on Masonite, acrylic, 33 × 43 inches, taken down from the wall for this play of shadows. Consequences: The artwork becomes the ground of a perceptual experiment between mother and child.
Sets for The Tower (costumes by Johns) and sets and costumes for Seven New Dances.

Two almost identical paintings demonstrate that brushwork, gestures included, is as repeatable as cut-and-pasted photographs. Two nearly twin canvases Consequences: Skepticism toward the gestural originality of Abstract Expressionism
Two almost identical paintings suggesting that the painterly gesture is as reproducible as cut-and-pasted photographs.

In the spring, dealers looking for new art visit Rauschenberg's studio, and he then takes them to see Johns's work; a positive, immediate, overwhelming reaction Consequences: Johns's show the following January; a succès de scandale for Rauschenberg in the spring of 1958
A composition for one to twenty pianists dedicated to the two artists; Cage's first significant venture into indeterminacy, music founded on the unrepeatable.
Duncan and his students carry on the theater workshop he led at Black Mountain, where he had written and produced his play Medea: The Maidenhead.
A photograph shows the community gathered for the announcement of the college's closing. A photograph kept in the University of Connecticut Archives

The college closes in 1957, an event described as traumatic; the influence of its former students and teachers is afterward immense. Consequences: A considerable afterlife of the BMC spirit in the American arts.

Dawson writes a story unique of its kind, Bloodstar, about the red-haired woman at BMC and the German woman who becomes the narrator, confronted at the end by the giant from the tower on the steps of the castle.

Besides Six Prayers, Anni makes a group of two panels for the Har Tzeon synagogue (Silver Spring, Maryland), at Marcel Breuer's request, based on a Star of David motif; in 1957, a group of eight panels for Temple Emanu-El in Dallas, in an abstract geometric design.

De Kooning begins a series in which figuration is at first entirely suppressed, inspired by the roads, highways, embankments, and billboards between the big city and its suburbs. Giant billboards, embankments, road shoulders, impeccably mowed lawns Consequences: He pursues his inquiry into painting as a medium

A Jewish refugee who fled Nazism and settled in Haifa, Heymann remembers Klee's classes as foundational: an experience of annihilation and resurrection, Klee's gaze turned toward his inner world, a luminous effect after the music.

The first of a long series of visiting teaching posts across the country; she now lives in New York only intermittently. There she begins the bullfight series, which will last six years. Bullfight paintings from 1957 to 1963: ink washes, watercolors, lithographs, oils, in formats from ten inches to ten feet Consequences: The beginning of twenty years of living apart from Bill

An exhibition covering the years 1925-1956, to travel to the Whitney Museum in the fall; Elaine de Kooning draws from it her essay “Stuart Davis: True to Life.” Davis is 63; the show covers 1925-1956; a previous retrospective at MoMA twelve years earlier, with works from 1912 on Consequences: The birth of the essay

Elaine de Kooning publishes a critical parody in the form of an interview with a fictitious painter, Adolf M. Pure, an “Anti-Post-Abstract-Impressionist,” whose art consists of rejecting colors, subject, straight lines, and working time. Pure paints black circles on foam rubber with an injection gun, on stretchers made of bicycle wheels; a painting finished in 45 minutes; he sleeps 16 hours a day.

The brothers push her belongings in wheelbarrows for more than twenty blocks; that very evening, a blast of music comes up through the floor; everyone drops everything and the brothers burst out laughing (the lease forbade living on the premises). Words: One brother: “This is a wonderful studio for an artist to go mad in”; Elaine tells of the general laughter Atmosphere: Laughter amid disaster, deafening music Stakes: Beginning a life alone in absurd conditions

On learning of the closing, the former student writes of his astonishment: in a still innocent corner of his heart, he had believed the college invincible. Words: “sad and uneasy and a few heartbeats nearer the grave” Atmosphere: Childhood mourning Stakes: The end of a belief

He goes out to buy cigarettes and supplies; she comes out of her building at the same moment, in four-inch platform shoes, tight pants, and a bright blouse; they walk together; he suggests a coffee, she chooses a drink; at the bar, they talk about poverty, and she quotes her mother; then the studio: she examines everything, arms folded, one hand pressing her arm against her breast, and even discovers a pile of papers the artist had never looked at; he does his Bogart routine with the cigarette and his James Dean routine against the wall; she comes and plants herself in front of him and they kiss Words: She quotes her mother: “Just take care of the luxuries, the necessities will take care themselves”; he feels himself in a state, finding her too good for him, royalty Atmosphere: Physical and moral excitement; the artist feels his anxiety dissolve and believes himself already an accomplished artist thanks to her Stakes: Elaine's magnetic power: turning a discouraged artist into a lover and a believer

Ginsberg reads a litany of imprecations, rising gradually from a murmur to a roar; the young audience catches fire (“the greatest”). After the reading, Goodman asks Allen what, in the ideas, the imagery, or the rhythm, made this crescendo probable; why a sequence, and why read that way. The poet is crestfallen and furious: the question had never occurred to him. Goodman concedes that during those minutes they shared the simple excitement of the rising voice, not a great poetic experience, but better than feeling nothing that night. Words: Goodman to Ginsberg: “You can't howl a gripe”; one can howl in pain or in rage, but what he is doing is griping. Atmosphere: The audience's collective warmth, a vocal crescendo, then the chill of the technical question Stakes: The birth of the Beat Generation judged by an elder who takes youth seriously enough to contradict it

A 21-year-old boy comes to Goodman's, his copy of On the Road in hand. An expressionless face, a square jaw, a fixed stare of unfelt hostility, molars grinding. When Goodman gives him attention, a small childlike smile splits his chapped lips. He explains that one must not commit oneself to any activity, for fear of making the wrong choice; Goodman answers that nothing can be interesting from coast to coast if one responds to it with no interest; all one gets is the activation of a stiff body in various cities. Words: Goodman: nothing can be interesting from coast to coast, boy, if he responds to it with no interest; all he gets are his “kicks.” Atmosphere: Domestic unease, attention at once clinical and affectionate Stakes: The failure of transmission between generations, and Goodman's determination to force it anyway

Cunningham shoots several rolls: in some frames Asawa, interrupted, looks up at baby Adam toddling toward the open window; in others he climbs onto her lap and sits in the open wire form, and she, improbably, keeps working; Cunningham will keep only the frame in which everyone is absorbed Atmosphere: Domestic, suspended, children and sculptures intertwined Stakes: The choice of a myth: showing absorption requires hiding the interruptions; the mother at work in calm modernity is a construction

Asawa, head bowed, works inside an open wire form; each child finds something to do (a book, a stick, a bottle); Cunningham chooses the shot in which the absorption is not interrupted. Atmosphere: A maternal pastoral, almost an allegory Stakes: The fantasy of a maternal bohemia in which modernism and motherhood are reconciled

The toddler Adam, sitting on the floor facing the painting AB.029 set at his height, raises his arm and casts his shadow toward his mother's outstretched hand; Cunningham photographs the moment. Atmosphere: Domestic intimacy, light casting shadows on the curved blue and green bands. Stakes: The mother's artwork becomes the child's perceptual playground.

In March, Olson goes to San Francisco for his Special View of History lectures; later in the month, a judge orders the educational programs halted until all debts are paid. Consequences: The end of academic activities.
Olson goes to San Francisco in March to deliver his Special View of History lectures.
At the end of March 1957, a judge orders the educational programs suspended until the debts are paid in full. Consequences: The effective closing of the college
Takes part in the exhibition.

Anni Albers writes a statement for the first annual conference of American craftsmen, later published in On Designing. A written statement submitted rather than a reported speech Consequences: The text becomes a plea for education through craft in a time of crisis

Preparing her contribution for Asilomar, she inspects the imaginary contents of her suitcase: toothbrush, raincoat, drip-dry clothes; no handmade object, no craftsman involved in their design for mass production. The observation grounds her argument: the craftsman must win back practical problems. Words: she admits that her drip-dry clothes are not handwoven Atmosphere: Lucid self-irony, a spirit of inventory Stakes: The craftsman facing the industrial world he has deserted
A selection of his works shown at the 4th Bienal

Shows portraits (Bill, Tom Hess, Harold Rosenberg, Frank O'Hara) and abstractions including Sympathizer, Protestant, Herzog, plus somber titles (Suicide, Vestibule Killing, The Death of Johnny A., after the 1952 murder of Johnny Acropolis, president of Teamsters Local 456 in Yonkers). Herzog: a stick figure with a triangular torso on a bright yellow and orange abstract ground, probably the mountaineer Maurice Herzog Consequences: James Schuyler notes the “rawness” and the “psychological insight”; the Arts Magazine critic praises a “masterly” execution
